newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMI says most EU states not ready for Euro.
newsitem.headline: EMI says most EU states not ready for Euro.

text.p: The European Monetary Institute on Wednesday said EU states were dragging their heels on getting their public finances in order for the planned 1999 launch of the Euro, and said most currently did not make the grade for monetary union.

In its first report of 1996 on EU states' efforts to meet single currency criteria, the EMI said: "Progress in fiscal consolidation has generally been too slow. Most countries have not yet achieved a situation which, in a broader view, might be judged as sustainable in the medium term."
"Overall, the report concludes that at present a majority of member states do not fulfil the necessary conditions for the adoption of a single currency," the EMI report said.

The Maastricht Treaty sets a reference value for national public deficits at three percent of GDP, a demand that has proved a major stumbling block for countries eager to take part in the Euro launch, even the powerhouse of Germany.

However the EMI added that recent forecasts suggested progress had been made in 1996 toward fiscal consolidation and that developments on exchange rates and price stability were favourable. These are the other key criteria for the union.

The EMI made no precise forecasts for 1997, the year on which the EU council will base its decision on which countries can join the Euro launch, but its report coincided with a report by the EU Commission which predicted that 12 of the 15 EU member states would make the Euro grade next year.
Nonetheless, the EMI said many European nations -- including Germany, France and Italy -- must make strong efforts to meet criteria for the single currency.
Italian debt and deficit levels remained unacceptably high, the EMI said, so that "very strong and sustained action is required" to get finances into line.

The EMI said it welcomed efforts to establish a stability pact to ensure fiscal discipline was maintained after EMU but added that this agreement, which would sanction errant nations, was no substitute for convincing budgetary consolidation.

One-off efforts to trim deficits were also not enough to to guarantee sustained fiscal discipline, the EMI warned. But the EMI did not make any reference to specific countries, such as France which plans to use France Telecom funds to lower its deficit.
"It is emphasised that the improvement of the deficit by measures with a one-off effect does not ensure sustainable consolidation," the report said.

The EMI also spoke out in support of the Maastricht Treaty's requirement for membership of the European Rate Mechanism (ERM) as a prelude to EMU participation, noting that a majority of members of the EMI council supported this.
The ERM membership requirement has attracted consistent criticism from Britain, whose currency is not part of the system.
